scenes.heading: Odd one out and classification
scenes.sub: Find the rule, find the misfit
scenes.say: Rose, tulip, oak, daisy. Which one doesn't belong? To answer, you need the exact rule that ties a group together. Let's learn how to find it fast.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Sorting the shopping into the right cupboards
scenes.science: Each word must fit the group's rule exactly
scenes.breaks: In a kitchen a jar can go in two cupboards. In a good question, only one word fits the rule.
scenes.say: Think about unpacking the shopping. Fruit goes in the bowl, tins in the cupboard. Anything that doesn't fit stands out. In these questions, you sort words by a rule, and the word that fits nowhere is the odd one out.

scenes.heading: Name the group exactly
steps: Say the rule as a sentence
scenes.say: Here's the method. Read every word first. Find three that clearly fit together. Say the rule as a sentence. Then test every word against it. The one that fails is the odd one out.

scenes.heading: Check in this order
points: Meaning: are they the same kind of thing?
Word type: all doing words? all describing?
scenes.say: Check meaning first: are they the same kind of thing? If not, check the word type. Are they all doing words, or all describing words? Last, check the letters. Are they made of the same letters, or spelled the same backwards?

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Odd one out: gently, kindly, lonely, swiftly
lines: All end in -ly: spelling won't help
scenes.say: Gently, kindly, lonely, swiftly. They all end in L Y, so spelling won't help. Try each one: she spoke gently, kindly, swiftly. All fine. She spoke lonely? No. Lonely describes a person, so it's the odd one out.

scenes.heading: Weak rule vs strong rule

right.title: Strong rule
points: You can say it in a sentence

scenes.say: Watch out for weak rules like word length, first letter or colour. A strong rule is about meaning, splits the words three against one, and you can say it in one clear sentence.
Recap. Read all the words first. Find three together and one alone. Check meaning, then word type, then letters. And remember, being on the same topic isn't enough. Now try the practice questions!
